name: Chapter 1: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
description: Anther, pollen, ovule, embryo sac, pollination, double fertilisation, endosperm, embryo, seed, fruit and apomixis

cards.term: Why are flowers important to a biologist?
cards.definition: They are morphological and embryological marvels and the sites of sexual reproduction
Cultivation of flowering plants for ornamental/commercial use (cut flowers, gardens)

cards.term: Two parts of a flower in which the two units of sexual reproduction develop?
cards.definition: Anther (pollen, male) and ovary/ovule (embryo sac, female)

cards.term: What happens in a plant long before a flower is seen?
cards.definition: The decision to flower is taken; hormonal and structural changes lead to differentiation of the floral primordium

cards.text: The {{c1::androecium}} (whorl of stamens) is the male reproductive organ; the {{c2::gynoecium}} is the female reproductive organ.
A stamen has a long slender stalk, the {{c1::filament}}, and a terminal, generally bilobed {{c2::anther}}.

cards.term: Where is the proximal end of the filament attached?
cards.definition: To the thalamus or the petal
Each anther lobe has two theca (a typical anther is bilobed and dithecous)

cards.term: What separates the two theca of a lobe?
cards.definition: A longitudinal groove running lengthwise

cards.term: Why is an anther called tetrasporangiate?
cards.definition: It is four-sided (tetragonal) with four microsporangia at the corners, two in each lobe
Pollen sacs: they run the length of the anther and are packed with pollen grains

cards.text: A microsporangium is surrounded by four wall layers: {{c1::epidermis}}, {{c1::endothecium}}, {{c1::middle layers}} and {{c1::tapetum}} (outer to inner).

cards.term: Function of the outer three wall layers of the microsporangium?
cards.definition: Protection and help in dehiscence of the anther to release pollen

cards.term: Innermost wall layer of the microsporangium, and its function?
cards.definition: Tapetum: nourishes the developing pollen grains
Dense cytoplasm and generally more than one nucleus

cards.term: How can tapetal cells become binucleate? (think)
cards.definition: Nuclear division (mitosis) without cytokinesis (or endomitosis/nuclear fusion)

cards.term: Role of the tapetum in forming the pollen wall? (Exercise 17)
cards.definition: It secretes sporopollenin precursors (and enzymes, Ubisch bodies) that build the exine; also nourishes microspores

cards.term: What occupies the centre of a young microsporangium?
cards.definition: Sporogenous tissue: compactly arranged homogenous cells

cards.term: Figure 1.3 · T.S. of young anther and one microsporangium

cards.definition: Formation of microspores from a pollen mother cell (PMC) by meiosis

cards.term: Why is each sporogenous cell a potential pollen mother cell?
cards.definition: Each can undergo meiosis to give a microspore tetrad

cards.term: Ploidy of the cells of a microspore tetrad?
cards.definition: Haploid (n) (products of meiosis)

cards.term: What makes microspores separate from the tetrad?
cards.definition: As anthers mature and dehydrate, microspores dissociate and develop into pollen grains
By dehiscence of the anther (along the line of dehiscence)
Mature dehisced anther (T.S.) releasing pollen grains

cards.term: Arrange in order: pollen grain, sporogenous tissue, microspore tetrad, pollen mother cell, male gametes (Exercise 3)
cards.definition: Sporogenous tissue → PMC → microspore tetrad → pollen grain → male gametes
The male gametophytes

cards.term: Shape and size of pollen grains?
cards.definition: Generally spherical, about 25–50 µm in diameter

cards.term: Identify: scanning electron micrographs of these structures.
cards.definition: Pollen grains of different species (Figure 1.4); note the varied exine patterns

cards.term: Outer wall layer of pollen, and what it is made of?
cards.definition: Exine, made of sporopollenin
One of the most resistant organic materials: withstands high temperature, strong acids and alkali; no enzyme is known to degrade it
Prominent apertures in the exine where sporopollenin is absent; the pollen tube emerges through one

cards.term: Why are pollen grains well-preserved as fossils?
cards.definition: Because of sporopollenin in the exine

cards.term: Why should the exine be hard? (think)
cards.definition: To protect the male gametophyte from drying, UV and damage during transfer

cards.term: Inner wall of pollen, and its composition?
cards.definition: Intine: thin, continuous, made of cellulose and pectin

cards.term: Two cells of a mature pollen grain?
cards.definition: Vegetative cell and generative cell
Vegetative: bigger, abundant food reserve, large irregular nucleus. Generative: small, spindle-shaped, dense cytoplasm, floats in the vegetative cell.

cards.term: In what % of angiosperms is pollen shed at the 2-celled stage?
cards.definition: Over 60%
Generative cell has divided mitotically into two male gametes before shedding

cards.term: Health problem caused by pollen of many species?
cards.definition: Allergies and bronchial afflictions: asthma, bronchitis

cards.term: Which weed causes pollen allergy in India, and how did it arrive?
cards.definition: Parthenium (carrot grass), as a contaminant with imported wheat
Pollen is rich in nutrients; claimed to boost performance of athletes and race horses

cards.term: On what does pollen viability depend?
cards.definition: Highly variable; partly on temperature and humidity

cards.term: How long does pollen of rice and wheat stay viable?
cards.definition: About 30 minutes after release

cards.term: Which families have pollen viable for months?
cards.definition: Some members of Rosaceae, Leguminosae and Solanaceae

cards.term: How is pollen stored for years? What is it used for?
cards.definition: In liquid nitrogen at −196°C; as pollen banks in crop breeding

cards.term: Correction: NCERT prints "-1960C" for liquid nitrogen. Correct value?
cards.definition: −196 °C (the degree sign was lost in printing)

cards.text: A gynoecium with a single pistil is {{c1::monocarpellary}}; with more than one it is {{c2::multicarpellary}}.
Fused pistils are {{c1::syncarpous}} (e.g. {{c2::Papaver}}); free pistils are {{c3::apocarpous}} (e.g. Michelia).
Three parts of a pistil: {{c1::stigma}} (landing platform for pollen), {{c2::style}} (slender part), {{c3::ovary}} (basal bulged part).

cards.definition: The ovarian cavity; the placenta lies inside it
Megasporangia

cards.text: Ovules per ovary: one in {{c1::wheat, paddy, mango}}; many in {{c2::papaya, watermelon, orchids}}.

cards.term: Figure 1.7 · Pistils of Hibiscus, Papaver, Michelia

cards.definition: (a) Hibiscus (single pistil); (b) multicarpellary syncarpous Papaver; (c) multicarpellary apocarpous Michelia
The stalk attaching the ovule to the placenta
Region where the body of the ovule fuses with the funicle (junction of ovule and funicle)
One or two protective envelopes of the ovule, encircling the nucellus
Small opening at the tip where integuments do not cover the nucellus
The basal part of the ovule, opposite the micropylar end
Mass of cells inside the integuments with abundant reserve food; contains the embryo sac

cards.term: How many embryo sacs does an ovule generally have, and from what?
cards.definition: One, formed from a megaspore
Formation of megaspores from the megaspore mother cell (MMC)

cards.term: Where does the MMC differentiate, and what is it like?
cards.definition: In the micropylar region of the nucellus; a large cell with dense cytoplasm and a prominent nucleus

cards.term: What does meiosis of the MMC produce?
cards.definition: Four megaspores (via a dyad, then a tetrad)

cards.term: Fate of the four megaspores in most flowering plants?
cards.definition: One is functional; the other three degenerate
Embryo sac formed from a single megaspore
Nucellus: 2n; MMC: 2n; Functional megaspore: n; Female gametophyte (embryo sac): n; Endosperm (PEN): 3n

cards.text: The functional megaspore nucleus divides mitotically to give {{c1::2}}, then {{c2::4}}, then {{c3::8}}-nucleate stages of the embryo sac.

cards.term: Why are the embryo-sac divisions called free nuclear?
cards.definition: Nuclear divisions are not followed immediately by cell wall formation

cards.term: When are cell walls laid down in the embryo sac?
cards.definition: After the 8-nucleate stage
The two nuclei not walled into cells; they lie below the egg apparatus in the large central cell

cards.text: The egg apparatus, at the {{c1::micropylar}} end, has two {{c2::synergids}} and one {{c2::egg cell}}.

cards.term: What is the filiform apparatus and its role?
cards.definition: Special cellular thickenings at the micropylar tip of the synergids; guide the pollen tube into a synergid

cards.term: Cells at the chalazal end of the embryo sac?
cards.definition: Three antipodals

cards.term: Why is the mature embryo sac "8-nucleate but 7-celled"?
cards.definition: 3 antipodals + 2 synergids + 1 egg = 6 cells, plus one central cell with two polar nuclei = 7 cells, 8 nuclei

cards.term: Mnemonic for the embryo sac (micropylar → chalazal)?
cards.definition: "2-1-2-3": 2 synergids + 1 egg at the micropyle, 2 polar nuclei in the middle, 3 antipodals at the chalaza = 8 nuclei

cards.term: Why do flowering plants need pollination?
cards.definition: Both male and female gametes are non-motile, so they must be brought together
Transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a pistil
Pollination within the same flower

cards.term: Why is complete autogamy rare in open flowers?
cards.definition: It needs synchrony of pollen release and stigma receptivity and anthers close to the stigma

cards.text: Viola, Oxalis and Commelina produce open {{c1::chasmogamous}} flowers and closed {{c2::cleistogamous}} flowers.

cards.definition: Flowers that do not open at all; anthers dehisce in the bud and pollinate the stigma

cards.term: Why are cleistogamous flowers invariably autogamous?
cards.definition: No chance of cross pollen landing on the stigma
Advantage: assured seed-set even without pollinators. Disadvantage: no variation, risk of inbreeding depression.
Pollen from anther to stigma of another flower of the same plant

cards.term: Geitonogamy is functionally cross-pollination but genetically like…?
cards.definition: Autogamy, because the pollen comes from the same plant
Pollen from anther to stigma of a different plant

cards.term: Only type of pollination bringing genetically different pollen?
cards.definition: Xenogamy
Abiotic: wind, water. Biotic: animals. Most plants use biotic agents.

cards.term: Why do wind/water-pollinated flowers make huge amounts of pollen?
cards.definition: Landing on the stigma is a chance event; extra pollen compensates for loss
Light, non-sticky pollen; well-exposed stamens; large, often feathery stigma; single ovule per ovary; many flowers in an inflorescence

cards.term: What are the "silk" threads of a corn cob?
cards.definition: The stigma and style, waving in the wind to trap pollen
Grasses
Rare: about 30 genera, mostly monocotyledons
Vallisneria, Hydrilla (fresh water); sea-grass Zostera (marine)

cards.term: Why is distribution of some bryophytes and pteridophytes limited?
cards.definition: They need water for transport of male gametes and fertilisation

cards.term: Do water hyacinth and water lily use water for pollination?
cards.definition: No. Flowers emerge above water and are pollinated by insects or wind
Female flower reaches the surface on a long stalk; male flowers/pollen released on the surface are carried passively by currents
Female flowers stay submerged; long, ribbon-like pollen is carried inside the water

cards.term: How is pollen of water-pollinated species protected from wetting?
cards.definition: A mucilaginous covering

cards.term: Why are wind/water-pollinated flowers not colourful and lack nectar?
cards.definition: They need not attract animals; making colour and nectar would waste energy
Bees, butterflies, flies, beetles, wasps, ants, moths, birds (sunbirds, hummingbirds), bats
Insects, particularly bees
Lemurs (primates), arboreal rodents, reptiles (gecko, garden lizard)
Large, colourful, fragrant, nectar-rich; small flowers clustered into an inflorescence

cards.term: Why do flowers pollinated by flies and beetles smell foul?
cards.definition: To attract these animals
Nectar and pollen grains

cards.term: How does an animal bring about pollination?
cards.definition: While harvesting rewards it touches anthers, gets coated in (sticky) pollen, then touches a stigma
Amorphophallus (~6 ft); reward is a safe place to lay eggs
Moth lays eggs in the ovary locule and pollinates the flower; larvae feed on developing seeds. Neither can complete its life cycle without the other.
Floral visitors that consume pollen/nectar without pollinating the flower

cards.term: Why do plants avoid continued self-pollination?
cards.definition: It leads to inbreeding depression

Pollen release and stigma receptivity not synchronised: Autogamy; Anther and stigma at different positions: Autogamy; Self-incompatibility: Self-fertilisation (autogamy + geitonogamy); Monoecy (castor, maize): Autogamy only, not geitonogamy; Dioecy (papaya): Both autogamy and geitonogamy

cards.definition: A genetic mechanism preventing self-pollen from fertilising ovules by inhibiting pollen germination or pollen-tube growth in the pistil
Monoecious: male and female flowers on the same plant (castor, maize). Dioecious: on different plants (papaya).

cards.term: Can a pistil tell right pollen from wrong pollen?
cards.definition: Yes. It recognises compatible pollen and accepts it; rejects incompatible pollen

cards.term: How does the pistil reject wrong pollen?
cards.definition: Prevents pollen germination on the stigma or pollen-tube growth in the style
Chemical components of the pollen interacting with those of the pistil

cards.term: Through what does a pollen tube emerge?
cards.definition: One of the germ pores

cards.term: In 2-celled pollen, when are the male gametes formed?
cards.definition: Generative cell divides during growth of the pollen tube in the stigma
Stigma → style → ovary → ovule via micropyle → a synergid via filiform apparatus
All events from pollen deposition on the stigma until pollen tubes enter the ovule

cards.term: Why does pollen-pistil interaction matter to breeders?
cards.definition: Manipulating it, even in incompatible pollinations, can yield desired hybrids

cards.term: How to see pollen germination in the lab?
cards.definition: Dust pollen (pea, chickpea, Crotalaria, balsam, Vinca) on ~10% sugar solution; observe after 15–30 min
Crossing chosen parents so only desired pollen reaches the stigma; a major crop-improvement approach
Removal of anthers from a bisexual flower bud before dehiscence, using forceps
Covering the emasculated flower with a bag (usually butter paper) to prevent contamination by unwanted pollen

cards.text: Artificial hybridisation: {{c1::emasculation}} → {{c2::bagging}} → dust desired pollen when stigma is receptive → {{c3::rebagging}}.

cards.term: Is emasculation needed if the female parent has unisexual flowers?
cards.definition: No. Female buds are simply bagged before opening, pollinated, then rebagged.

cards.term: What happens after the pollen tube enters a synergid?
cards.definition: It releases the two male gametes into the synergid cytoplasm
Fusion of one male gamete with the egg → diploid zygote
Fusion of the second male gamete with the two polar nuclei → triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN)
In the central cell of the embryo sac
Occurrence of syngamy + triple fusion in one embryo sac; unique to flowering plants

cards.text: After triple fusion the central cell becomes the {{c1::primary endosperm cell (PEC)}}, which develops into the {{c2::endosperm}}; the zygote develops into the {{c3::embryo}}.

cards.term: Why is it called "fertilisation" if triple fusion forms no embryo? (intuition)
cards.definition: Both fusions involve a male gamete; one builds the baby (embryo), the other builds its lunch box (endosperm)
Endosperm and embryo development, maturation of ovules → seeds and ovary → fruit

cards.term: Why does endosperm develop before the embryo?
cards.definition: To give assured nutrition to the developing embryo
Triploid (3n); stores reserve food for the developing embryo
PEN divides repeatedly into free nuclei without walls; later walls form and it becomes cellular

cards.text: Tender coconut water is {{c1::free-nuclear}} endosperm; the white kernel is {{c2::cellular}} endosperm.

cards.term: Seeds where endosperm is fully consumed before maturity?
cards.definition: Pea, groundnut, beans
Castor and coconut (also cereals: wheat, rice, maize)
At the micropylar end of the embryo sac, where the zygote lies

cards.term: Why does the zygote remain dormant for a while? (Exercise 12)
cards.definition: It divides only after some endosperm forms, ensuring nutrition for the embryo
(a) Fertilised embryo sac with zygote and PEN; (b) stages of dicot embryo development

cards.term: Are early embryo stages different in monocots and dicots?
cards.definition: No; early embryogeny is similar in both

cards.term: Parts of a typical dicot embryo?
cards.definition: An embryonal axis and two cotyledons
Epicotyl: Axis above the cotyledons; ends in the plumule (stem tip); Hypocotyl: Axis below the cotyledons; ends in the radicle (root tip)

advancedHtml.backHtml:
Exercise 13a

What is it?

EpicotylAxis above the cotyledons; ends in the plumule (stem tip)
HypocotylAxis below the cotyledons; ends in the radicle (root tip)

cards.term: What covers the root tip of the embryo?
cards.definition: A root cap

cards.term: Figure 1.14 · Dicot embryo and grass embryo
Cotyledon of the grass family called?
cards.definition: Scutellum, lateral to the embryonal axis
Coleorhiza: Radicle and root cap; Coleoptile: Shoot apex and a few leaf primordia

advancedHtml.backHtml:
Exercise 13b

What does it sheath?

ColeorhizaRadicle and root cap
ColeoptileShoot apex and a few leaf primordia

cards.term: In a grass embryo, the epicotyl is the axis above…?
cards.definition: The level of attachment of the scutellum

cards.term: Correction: NCERT prints "radical" on p. 20. Correct word?
cards.definition: Radicle (the embryonic root); "radical" means something else
The final product of sexual reproduction; often described as a fertilised ovule
Seed coat(s), cotyledon(s), embryo axis
They store food reserves
No residual endosperm (consumed during embryo development): pea, groundnut
Retain part of the endosperm: wheat, maize, barley, castor
Residual, persistent nucellus in the seed: black pepper, beet
Testa (seed coat): Integuments of the ovule; Perisperm: Nucellus (persisting); Pericarp (fruit wall): Ovary wall

Develops from?

Testa (seed coat)?
Perisperm?
Pericarp (fruit wall)?

Develops from?

PerispermNucellus (persisting)

cards.term: Role of the micropyle in a seed?
cards.definition: Remains as a small pore that lets oxygen and water in during germination

cards.term: Moisture content of a mature seed?
cards.definition: 10–15% by mass
State of inactivity of the embryo as the seed dries; it germinates when conditions become favourable
Adequate moisture, oxygen and suitable temperature
Fleshy: guava, orange, mango. Dry: groundnut, mustard.
Fruits where the thalamus also contributes: apple, strawberry, cashew

cards.term: Why is apple a false fruit? (Exercise 14)
cards.definition: The fleshy edible part develops from the thalamus, not only the ovary
Fruits that develop only from the ovary
Fruits developed without fertilisation: seedless, e.g. banana; inducible with growth hormones

cards.term: Which fruits would you choose for induced parthenocarpy? (Exercise 16)
cards.definition: Fruits eaten for their flesh with many/hard seeds: orange, lemon, watermelon, grapes, guava (seedless is preferred)
Pollination and fertilisation independent of water; better dispersal; food reserve for seedlings; hard coat protects embryo; new genetic combinations

cards.term: Why are dehydration and dormancy crucial for agriculture?
cards.definition: They allow storage of seeds as food all year and for the next crop
Lupinus arcticus from Arctic tundra: germinated after ~10,000 years
Date palm, Phoenix dactylifera, from King Herod’s palace near the Dead Sea

cards.term: Plants whose fruits contain thousands of tiny seeds?
cards.definition: Orchids, parasitic Orobanche and Striga
Production of seeds without fertilisation: asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction
Some species of Asteraceae and grasses
Apomixis: seed without fertilisation. Parthenocarpy: fruit without fertilisation (seedless).
A diploid egg forms without reduction division and develops into an embryo without fertilisation
Nucellar cells around the embryo sac divide, protrude into it and develop into embryos
More than one embryo in a seed, e.g. orange (Citrus), mango
Genetically identical to the mother: they are clones
Must be produced every year; seeds from hybrids segregate and lose hybrid characters; costly for farmers

cards.term: Why is apomixis important to the hybrid seed industry?
cards.definition: Apomictic hybrids show no segregation, so farmers can reuse hybrid seed year after year

cards.term: Why does an apomictic hybrid not segregate? (intuition)
cards.definition: No meiosis and no fertilisation: every seed is a photocopy of the hybrid mother
Mother cell: PMC vs MMC; Division: Meiosis in both; Product: Microspore tetrad → pollen vs 4 megaspores (1 functional); Gametophyte: Pollen grain vs embryo sac
